newsitem.title: USA: Fed uneasy about forex swaps but won't change them.
newsitem.headline: Fed uneasy about forex swaps but won't change them.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The Federal Reserve is not altogether happy with the $35 billion network of currency swaps that it has in place with overseas central banks to support intervention in the foreign exchange market, Fed sources said.
But, they added, the Fed looks unlikely to do anything about pruning back or eliminating the little-used bilateral credit lines anytime soon.
If they were starting off from scratch, Fed policymakers probably would never have entered into the elaborate system of swaps, many of them with countries in Europe, the sources said.

But diplomatic and other reasons argue against scrapping or radically altering the network at this time, even though a hard core of central bank policymakers consider the swaps -- and the intervention they support -- counterproductive.

The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) discussed the swap arrangements at a policy-setting meeting on July 2-3, but, according to the published minutes of that gathering, made no decision on what to do about them.
"The Committee considered ... whether the swap arrangements, all of which had been put in place in the 1960s, remained an appropriate approach," the FOMC said.
But, it added, "The Committee made no decision relating to these matters, though it was understood that these issues would be explored further."

The Fed has swap lines with about 15 nations. The biggest are with Mexico and Germany, at $6 billion each, and Japan, at $5 billion. But other less influential countries, among them Austria and Denmark, also have credit lines.
With the exception of Mexico, which drew on its swap arrangement in 1995 to help it weather a currency crisis, little use has been made of the credit lines in recent years.
But Fed sources, who declined to be named, said it would be hard to eliminate some of the swap lines, if only because that might ruffle the feathers of the allies concerned.

The discussion within the Fed about the usefulness of the swaps is symptomatic of a broader debate that has been going on for years at the central bank about its participation in Treasury-led currency market operations.

A minority of Fed policymakers view intervention as a distraction at best and counterproductive at worst. Others take a more benign view, the sources said, and consider it useful at best and harmless at worst.
The debate took on a harder edge last year after the Treasury tapped resources afforded by the Fed to bypass Congress and engineer an economic rescue of Mexico.
Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus has made perhaps the most comprehensive public case among FOMC members against currency intervention by the U.S. central bank.

Writing in his organization's annual report this year, Broaddus and his research director Martin Goodfriend argued that intervention compromises the Fed's credibility as an inflation fighter by raising questions about its goals.
"The Fed's participation in foreign exchange policy with the Treasury creates doubt about whether monetary policy will support domestic or external objectives," they said.
"This doubt undermines the credibility of the Fed's longer-term objective of reducing and ultimately eliminating inflation," Broaddus and Goodfriend added.
They also maintained that Fed participation in such operations as the Mexican bail-out could hurt the central bank by raising questions in Congress about its independence.
But that view does not seem to be shared by many other Fed officials, including central bank Chairman Alan Greenspan, who was a proponent of the Mexican rescue package.
Greenspan argued in favor of continued Fed participation in Treasury-led currency intervention at an FOMC meeting as far back as March 1990.

At that time, according to recently-released transcripts of the meeting, Greenspan maintained that the central bank would lose influence if it did not take part in intervention and left it to the Treasury on its own.
He and other Fed policymakers at that meeting though also made clear their distaste for -- and opposition to -- any effort to drive the dollar down across the board.
